text: Consider a city that wants to reroute delivery vehicles when a road becomes unavailable, a bridge is restricted, or a new incident changes expected travel time. A static shortest-path calculation is insufficient because travel times depend on the time of day, vehicle capacity, service deadlines, and information that may arrive while a route is already in progress. The planning system maintains a versioned road graph, records the source and confidence of each incident report, and predicts several plausible future states rather than treating one forecast as certain. A controller evaluates candidate routes against hard constraints first, then compares cost, lateness, distance, and stability. When new information arrives, it reuses the previous solution as a warm start but still checks feasibility from scratch. In evaluation, every baseline receives the same incident stream, compute budget, and stopping condition. The report includes failed routes and delayed updates, because excluding difficult cases would make the proposed method appear more reliable than it is.

A scientific benchmark is useful only when its protocol is precise enough for an independent team to reproduce. The dataset manifest should identify the source version, preprocessing steps, split boundaries, random seeds, software versions, and any records excluded before training. Normalization statistics must be estimated on the training partition rather than on the entire dataset, and duplicate or near-duplicate examples should not cross from training into evaluation. If a model is tuned repeatedly against the final test set, that set has become part of the development process even if its labels remain hidden. The benchmark should therefore retain a separate validation set, publish the scoring script, and include uncertainty estimates across independent runs. A higher mean score is not automatically meaningful when the variance is large or when the evaluation sample is too small to resolve the difference. Negative results, failed configurations, and compute constraints belong in the record alongside the strongest successful run.

For a numerical sanity check, let the measured vector be x = [0.12, -0.07, 1.25, 0.00, -3.5] and the perturbed vector be x′ = x + ε, where ε is small but not necessarily independent across coordinates. Report the absolute error, relative L2 error, maximum coordinate change, and the number of values that changed representation; do not collapse these quantities into one undocumented score. A histogram can hide a local pattern, while a local correlation test can miss a global shift, so the analysis should use complementary measurements and state their limitations. When a metric is undefined because the reference norm is zero, record that case explicitly instead of inserting a convenient value. The same rule applies to detector evaluation: report class balance, confidence intervals, the false-positive operating point, and the held-out split. Reproducibility depends as much on exposing these decisions as on publishing the final number.
